query: For nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially crystallized as a solid solution, what governs whether structural and chemical stability is maintained across catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges of 473–1923 K? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled comparison, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, define the conditions under which the prediction should hold, identify supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Structural and chemical stability in high-entropy nanoparticles over 473–1923 K is maintained when the overall inter-elemental mixing enthalpy is near optimal (i.e., modest in magnitude), allowing the high configurational entropy of a near-equiatomic solid solution to counteract any tendencies toward segregation or intermetallic formation.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios that are initially crystallized as a single-phase solid solution.
generation.intervention: Systematically modify the alloy composition to slightly alter the overall mixing enthalpy while keeping near-equiatomic ratios intact, then expose these nanoparticles to controlled thermal cycles spanning 473–1923 K under catalytic/thermoelectric operating conditions.
generation.conditions: Experiments performed in inert or controlled reactive atmospheres that mimic catalytic and thermoelectric environments, with heating ramps and hold times that allow equilibrium to be approached but minimize kinetic overprinting.
generation.structural_mediator: The balance between modest (near optimal) mixing enthalpy and high configurational entropy that stabilizes the single-phase structure, preventing phase separation or the formation of intermetallic compounds.
generation.mechanism: If the mixing enthalpy is not too exothermic or endothermic, the configurational entropy dominates at elevated temperatures and stabilizes the homogeneous solid solution. Deviations from this balance result in an energetic driving force for the nucleation of secondary phases or chemical segregation, thereby degrading structural and chemical stability.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles designed with optimal mixing enthalpy will retain their single-phase, homogeneously mixed state with minimal segregation or intermetallic formation across the temperature range, preserving catalytic/thermoelectric performance. In contrast, nanoparticles with deliberately perturbed (non-optimal) mixing enthalpy will display detectable phase separation or chemical changes and diminished performance.
generation.baseline: The as-synthesized particles, initially confirmed as single-phase solid solutions at ambient conditions.
generation.boundary: This prediction is expected to hold when kinetic effects such as rapid diffusion do not override the equilibrium thermodynamic stabilization and when external factors (e.g., aggressive oxidation) are controlled; under extreme reactive conditions, additional degradation pathways may dominate.
generation.uncertainty: Precise quantification of the optimal mixing enthalpy window is still uncertain, and catalytic versus thermoelectric operational kinetics might introduce additional effects not solely captured by equilibrium thermodynamics.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two series of HEA nanoparticles: one series with compositions optimized for near-zero (or modest) mixing enthalpy and a second series where one or more elements are adjusted to yield a more highly negative or positive mixing enthalpy without drastically changing the overall equiatomic nature. Subject both series to a heat treatment protocol spanning 473–1923 K under inert/controlled catalytic or thermoelectric conditions. Use X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) to monitor phase purity and elemental distributions at several temperature steps.
measurements: XRD patterns to identify the emergence of secondary phases or intermetallic compounds
TEM imaging and EDS mapping for nanoscale compositional homogeneity versus segregation
Catalytic activity or thermoelectric performance measurements before and after thermal cycling
Surface chemical state analyses (e.g., XPS) for signs of oxidation or phase separation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, under controlled conditions, the nanoparticles engineered for optimal mixing enthalpy exhibit similar or greater degrees of phase segregation, chemical decomposition, or performance loss compared to the deliberately perturbed (non-optimal) samples, then the hypothesis—that optimal mixing enthalpy governs the maintained structural and chemical stability—is falsified.

A map of single-phase high-entropy alloys

Abstract: AbstractHigh-entropy alloys have exhibited unusual materials properties. The stability of equimolar single-phase solid solution of five or more elements is supposedly rare and identifying the existence of such alloys has been challenging because of the vast chemical space of possible combinations. Herein, based on high-throughput density-functional theory calculations, we construct a chemical map of single-phase equimolar high-entropy alloys by investigating over 658,000 equimolar quinary alloys through a binary regular solid-solution model. We identify 30,201 potential single-phase equimolar alloys (5% of the possible combinations) forming mainly in body-centered cubic structures. We unveil the chemistries that are likely to form high-entropy alloys, and identify the complex interplay among mixing enthalpy, intermetallics formation, and melting point that drives the formation of these solid solutions. We demonstrate the power of our method by predicting the existence of two new high-entropy alloys, i.e. the body-centered cubic AlCoMnNiV and the face-centered cubic CoFeMnNiZn, which are successfully synthesized.Subject terms: Mat

High Entropy Alloys Mined From Binary Phase Diagrams

Abstract: High entropy alloys (HEA) are a new type of high-performance structural material. Their vast degrees of compositional freedom provide for extensive opportunities to design alloys with tailored properties. However, compositional complexities present challenges for alloy design. Current approaches have shown limited reliability in accounting for the compositional regions of single solid solution and composite phases. For the first time, a phenomenological method analysing binary phase diagrams to predict HEA phases is presented. The hypothesis is that the HEA structural stability is encoded within the phase diagrams. Accordingly, we introduce several phase-diagram inspired parameters and employ machine learning (ML) to classify 600+ reported HEAs based on these parameters. Compared to other large database statistical prediction models, this model gives more detailed and accurate phase predictions. Both the overall HEA prediction and specifically single-phase HEA prediction rate are above 80%.
